title: I'm from Indonesia
goal: Say where you're from, name nationalities and languages, and meet two endings you'll use every day: -დან (from) and -ად (in / -ly).
bekal: name countries and cities with the ending -დან
say which languages you speak, with the ending -ად
say how well: ცოტა, კარგად, საერთოდ არა

dialogs.title: დიალოგი — In the coffee queue
dialogs.intro: Ani is queuing for coffee and chatting with Levan, the man in front of her. Notice how the country name changes its ending as soon as it answers "where from" — and how the language name changes its ending again as soon as the talk turns to speaking.

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: Excuse me, are you a tourist?

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: No, I'm a student. I'm learning Georgian.

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: From Indonesia?! That's very far. I'm Levan, I'm Georgian.
lines.literal: Indonesia-from?! very — far-is. I — Levan — am, Georgian.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. Are you from Tbilisi?

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: No, from Batumi. You speak Georgian well!

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Oh no, I know a little. Do you speak English?

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: A little. My Russian is better.

lines.speaker: ლევანი:
lines.id: Excellent! How do you say „gamarjoba“ in Indonesian?

notes: **-დან means "from", and it sticks straight onto the place name.** A final -ი drops first: თბილის**ი** → თბილის**იდან**, ბათუმ**ი** → ბათუმ**იდან**. Names ending in -ა change it to -ი: ჯაკარტ**ა** → ჯაკარტ**იდან**, ინდონეზი**ა** → ინდონეზი**იდან** (note the two ი in a row — that's right, and both are pronounced).

**Nationalities are formed with -ელი, and very neatly.** ინდონეზია → ინდონეზი**ელი** (Indonesian person), ამერიკა → ამერიკ**ელი**, იტალია → იტალი**ელი**, ჩინეთი → ჩინ**ელი**. ⚠️ Some of the most common ones are irregular and must be memorized: **ქართველი** (Georgian), **რუსი** (Russian), **ინგლისელი** (English), **ბერძენი** (Greek).

**Language names are formed with -ური or -ული**, and they're different words from the nationality. ქართველი = a Georgian person, ქართ**ული** = the Georgian language. ინდონეზი**ელი** = an Indonesian, ინდონეზი**ური** = Indonesian (the language). ინგლის**ური**, რუს**ული**, ესპან**ური**, ჩინ**ური**.

**And as soon as you talk "in" that language, the ending changes again to -ად.** ქართული → ქართულ**ად** ვლაპარაკობ (I speak in Georgian). ⚠️ A classic trap: English says "I speak Georgian" with no extra word, so learners write *ქართული ვლაპარაკობ*, which sounds like "I talk about the Georgian language" — the thing, not the tool. The -ად ending turns it into "in Georgian".

**ქართულს ვსწავლობ — why the -ს ending?** Because in this sentence Georgian is the **object** of the action: the thing being learned. A noun that is the object takes -ს. You don't need to learn this yet; just note that Georgian nouns change their ending according to their role, and unit 9 covers it calmly.

**"You speak Georgian well!" — you'll hear this constantly, and almost always too early.** The right response isn't a strong denial but **არა, ცოტა ვიცი** (oh, I know a little) or **მადლობა, ვსწავლობ** (thanks, I'm learning). Overdoing the denial actually sounds odd.

**ვილაპარაკოთ = "let's speak".** The Georgian "let's" form uses the ending **-ოთ**: წავიდე**თ** (let's go), ვჭამო**თ** (let's eat), დავლიო**თ** (let's drink). Just recognize the pattern for now; unit 15 uses it for real.

grammars.title: Country, people, and language — three words from one root
body: These three columns are the only important thing to memorize in this unit. Read across, not down: what needs to stick is how the three relate to each other.
after: ⚠️ **საქართველო has nothing to do with the word "Georgia".** Georgians call their country Sakartvelo and themselves kartveli — the name "Georgia" came from outside, through Persian and Greek. Saying საქართველო correctly is the quickest way to show you're not just another tourist.

grammars.title: How well? Four honest answers
body: All of these use the verb **ვლაპარაკობ** (I speak) or **ვიცი** (I know), and only the word in front of it changes.

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: I don't know any Georgian at all

after: The last sentence is the most useful. It explains and asks for patience at the same time, and almost always makes people slow down.

sections.title: Asking where someone's from, three levels deep

blocks.text: A first conversation with a Georgian almost always walks down this ladder: country, city, then "how long have you been here".

head: Question
Say it
It asks
rows: how long you've been in Georgia

blocks.title: Three answers that always work
items: **ინდონეზიიდან ვარ.** — a safe answer for anyone, anywhere.
**ინდონეზიიდან ვარ, ჯაკარტიდან.** — answers the city too. Georgians generally know Bali far better than Jakarta; *ბალი იცით? ეს ინდონეზიაა.* opens a lot of conversations.
⚠️ Don't answer *მე ინდონეზია ვარ* — that means "I am the country of Indonesia". The correct forms are **ინდონეზიიდან ვარ** (from) or **ინდონეზიელი ვარ** (the nationality).

blocks.text: One thing that may surprise you: the question "how long have you been here" is often followed by a dinner invitation. That's not small talk. Hospitality to guests in Georgia has its own saying — *სტუმარი ღვთისაა* (st'umari ghvtisaa), "a guest is God's" — and unit 19 explores it further.

საიდან ხართ? — ინდონეზიიდან ვარ, ჯაკარტიდან. — ინდონეზიელი ვარ. — ქართულად ცოტა ვლაპარაკობ. — ქართულს ვსწავლობ. — ინგლისურად ლაპარაკობთ?
